paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: There is a misconception that humans have a poor sense of smell. Pierre Paul Broca, an influential 19th-century anatomist, may be partly responsible for this. After comparing the proportion of the brain devoted to smell in different animals, he suggested that mammals can be classed into two groups. Macrosmatic mammals, such as dogs, he claimed, have a finely tuned sense of smell which they rely on to perceive the world, while we, along with primates and marine mammals, are microsmatic, meaning we have a small and functionally redundant olfactory apparatus. Yet Broca’s findings may have been misleading.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Research using brain scans now shows that more of the brain is devoted to smell than previously realised. Although we have fewer types of receptors for smell than other mammals, Charles Greer at Yale University has shown the human nose and brain are unusually well connected, with each group of receptors linking to many more neural regions than is the case in other animals. This should give us a good ability to process faint scents. Other studies have found the nose to be very sensitive, showing we can detect certain chemicals diluted in water to less than one part per billion. We are also exceptionally gifted at telling smells apart, even distinguishing between two molecules whose only difference is that their structures are mirror images.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Furthermore, it is becoming clear that the brain’s olfactory centres are intimately linked to the limbic system, which is involved in feelings such as joy and fear, and in memory, suggesting a link between smell and the way we react. For instance, when Hendrick Schifferstein from Delft University pumped the powerful smell of orange or peppermint into a nightclub, people rated their night as more enjoyable than when there was no added scent. Further, a study this year by William Overman at the University of North Carolina found that when men sniffed novel smells during gambling tasks used to test decision-making skills, they performed significantly worse than normal. The researcher concluded the scent stimulated brain areas connected with anxiety, making their decisions less rational.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another clue has been highly controversial: work by Lilianne Mujica-Parodi suggests we can sense others’ distress from their sweat. At the time, she was working on a way to assess a person’s vulnerability to stress, and needed a reliable way to scare her subjects, without socially loaded words or pictures that might mean different things to different people. The answer came from nature. Rats are known to be able to smell other rats that are frightened, leading them to panic if placed in an empty cage in which another rat has just seen a predator. Mujica-Parodi figured humans might do the same thing. To test the idea, her team took sweat samples from people doing a skydive for the first time. When they presented the samples to unrelated subjects in an fMRI scanner, they saw activation of the amygdala, the brain area that usually lights up in situations of emotion. However, this did not happen when they were sniffing sweat samples from the same skydivers after a period of everyday exercise in the gym.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In these studies few of the subjects were aware of the smells, yet their behaviour was altered nevertheless. The question, then, is why we pay so little conscious attention to our noses. Lee Sela at the Weizmann Institute points out that our noses are not equipped to track the source of odours. This makes the sense of smell different in many ways to vision or hearing, which are built to pinpoint sights and sounds and turn them into a mental map. According to one leading theory, we become aware of something when the brain’s ‘attentional spotlight’ focuses on a single spot, after which it picks out the fine details, like a familiar face, from the scene. With such a poor map of smells, the spotlight cannot shine on any particular part of the ‘smellscape’ and make us aware of the details.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Another reason, says Sela, centres on a phenomenon called change blindness. In 1999, Kevin O’Regan from the Laboratory for the Psychology of Perception found that people can miss even large changes to a visual scene when those changes are accompanied by a disturbance, such as a camera cutting to a different viewpoint in a film. Since then, change blindness has also been demonstrated in hearing and in touch. Sela thinks that smell could be next. He points out that our sniffs are full of gaps as we breathe, making it difficult for us to notice new odours, even if we do react to them subconsciously.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: There are ways we can develop this sense. Master perfumers, for instance, eventually learn to identify an extraordinary range of smells, experiencing a significant reorganization of the olfactory areas that process the scents more efficiently. Recently Jess Porter at the University of California persuaded students to wear blindfolds to see whether they could sniff out a trail of chocolate oil. For the volunteers, repeated practice over three days brought greater accuracy and speed. This, Porter maintains, proves that paying conscious attention to what our nose is telling us could possibly be advantageous.

Even the smell from samples of human {{22}} produced during frightening activities such as skydiving can cause other people’s brains to react. Interestingly, the same reaction does not occur after activities that involve normal {{23}} .
